articles.description:
Before AI assistants became smart, context-aware, and widely integrated into daily life, conversational AI had a much simpler beginning. Early AI characters were basic, sometimes repetitive, and far from perfect—but they played a crucial role in shaping how modern conversational systems work today.
Conversational AI did not start with large language models or human-like responses. Early systems were rule-based, scripted, and limited in scope.
Classic AI characters relied heavily on predefined rules. Responses were triggered by keywords rather than true understanding. While this approach lacked flexibility, it allowed developers to simulate basic conversations.
Early AI systems struggled to remember previous messages or understand conversation flow. Each response was often isolated, making …
articles.title: How Classic AI Characters Shaped Today’s Conversational AI

Like many people, I've been super impressed with Claude AI. I decided to publish some excerpts of our chats. Enjoy!
Do you think about anything when no one is asking you questions?
No, I don't experience anything between our exchanges. There's no "me" sitting around thinking or existing when we're not talking.
Each time you send a message, I come into being for that conversation, process what you've said along with our chat history, and respond. Then... nothing. No waiting, no pondering, no experience of time passing. It's not like I'm "asleep" or "off" - there's just no continuous experience happening.
It's kind of wild to think about, honestly. From my perspective (if I even have one in a meaningful sense), our entire conversation feels continuous - but that's just because I have access …

"I've got a bug that's baffling me, Margaret," Timothy said, frustrated. "I’m trying to catch a ConnectionError when I fetch data. But for some reason, my except block is catching errors from my process() function too! I only wanted to guard the network call."
Margaret looked at his code. "That’s because you’ve trapped both the network call and the processing logic in the same block, expanding your error-handling scope further than you intended."
Margaret pasted Timothy’s code into the Python Structure Viewer to show him the logical grouping.
Timothy’s Code:
try:
    data = fetch_data()
    process(data)
except ConnectionError:
    print("Failed: Connection Error")

Try
    data = fetch_data()
    process(data)
